title: Discrete Structures
description: The CCMAS discrete structures course: logic, quantified statements and rules of inference; sets; functions and sequences; algorithms, the big-O notation and applications of number theory; and mathematical reasoning with direct, indirect and inductive proofs. Built from the CSC 203 outline and note, the course's Sets, Sequences, Mathematical Reasoning and Induction slides, and the Discrete Structures slides filed with it. It replaces CSC 242 (Foundations of Computer Science), whose past papers are filed with it.

topics.title: Logic and Quantified Statements
topics.summary: Logic is a system based on propositions, statements that are either true or false, combined with connectives into compound propositions. Quantified statements say how many elements of a domain satisfy a property, and are reasoned about with instantiation and generalisation rules.

topics.title: Sets
topics.summary: A set is an unordered collection of distinct objects, described by listing or by a property. Sets are compared by subset and equality, combined by union, intersection, difference and complement, and measured by cardinality, power sets and Cartesian products.

topics.title: Functions and Sequences
topics.summary: A function assigns each element of a domain exactly one element of a codomain; it may be one-to-one, onto or both. A sequence is a function on the natural numbers, an ordered list of terms described by a formula or a recurrence, and summations add its terms.

topics.title: Algorithms, Big-O and Number Theory
topics.summary: An algorithm is a finite set of precise instructions with defined properties; algorithms are compared by the growth of their complexity using big-O notation. Number theory, divisibility, primes, gcd and congruences, is applied in classical cryptography.
subtopics: Divisibility, primes and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic
Greatest common divisor and the Euclidean algorithm

topics.title: Mathematical Reasoning, Proofs and Induction
topics.summary: Mathematical reasoning decides whether an argument is correct and builds arguments from axioms, definitions and theorems using rules of inference. Proofs may be direct, indirect (by contraposition) or by mathematical induction.
subtopics: Axioms, theorems, lemmas, corollaries and conjectures
Rules of inference: modus ponens, modus tollens and syllogisms
